sermons.life_context: Moody was an unpaid city missionary in Chicago. He was active in the Illinois Street Church, which grew out of his mission, and had become the city's YMCA president in 1866. The year before, he had met the singer Ira Sankey at a YMCA convention in Indianapolis. The Great Chicago Fire that began that night destroyed Farwell Hall, the church and his home.

Moody was leading his Chicago campaign, which began in October 1876 after missions in Brooklyn, Philadelphia and New York. When he came back from Britain in August 1875 he had bought a small farm near his mother's home in Northfield. Two days earlier the singer P. P. Bliss and his wife had died in the Ashtabula bridge disaster while travelling to join this mission.

Moody was still leading his Chicago campaign, which began in October 1876. A week earlier the singer P. P. Bliss and his wife had died in the Ashtabula bridge disaster while travelling to join it. His Boston campaign followed in 1877, and the tract's heading says he repeated this sermon at the Boston Tabernacle on 29 April.

No delivery date is recorded, and the collection was entered for copyright in 1880. By then Moody's third child, Paul, had been born (April 1879). Northfield Seminary for young women had opened in November 1879, with its first classes held in the dining room of his Northfield home. The first Northfield conference followed in 1880.

No delivery date is recorded, and the collection this sermon opens was entered for copyright in 1880. By then Moody had been home from his 1873–75 British campaign for about five years. He had led city campaigns in Brooklyn, Philadelphia, New York, Chicago and Boston. His Northfield Seminary for young women opened in November 1879, with its first classes held in his Northfield home.

The text's imagined note is dated July 1880. That came after Moody's American city campaigns in Brooklyn, Philadelphia, New York, Chicago (1876) and Boston (1877). He had bought a farm at Northfield after coming back from Britain in 1875. Northfield Seminary for young women opened there in November 1879, and the first Northfield conference followed in 1880.

Moody was leading the New York campaign at the Hippodrome. It followed missions in Brooklyn from October 1875 and then in Philadelphia, after his two-year British campaign with Ira Sankey. When he returned in August 1875 he bought a small farm near his mother's home at Northfield, which gradually became the family home.

Moody gave this prayer-meeting talk during his New York campaign at the Hippodrome. That campaign followed his missions in Brooklyn and Philadelphia after he came home from Britain in August 1875. On his return he bought a small farm near his mother's home in Northfield, which gradually became the family home.

Moody's preface says the book draws on addresses he gave in British and American cities. It appeared in 1884, the last year of his second British mission (1881–84), whose long London campaign began in November 1883. At home in Northfield he had opened Mount Hermon School for boys in 1881.

No delivery date is recorded. The book was published in 1884, the last year of Moody's second British mission (1881–84), which included a long London campaign from November 1883. He worked from Northfield, where he had founded a seminary for young women (1879) and Mount Hermon School for boys (1881).

Revell published this collection in 1884, the last year of Moody's second British mission (1881–84), which included a long London campaign from November 1883. He worked from Northfield, where Mount Hermon School had opened in 1881. The address's story of burying poor children from his Sunday school draws on his earlier Chicago mission work.

Revell issued the book in 1896, the year Moody's mother died. In autumn 1892 a London doctor had found a heart irregularity, and that November Moody survived the disabled steamer Spree. Since then he had led the 1893 World's Fair campaign in Chicago and kept up city missions and Northfield conferences.

The book was copyrighted in 1898, two years after Moody's mother died, while he was still holding city missions and Northfield conferences. Late that year, on 30 November, his only grandson and namesake, Dwight, died while Moody was in Colorado.

Moody was on his first long British campaign with Ira Sankey. He had landed at Liverpool with his family on 17 June 1873 and found that all three of his sponsors had died. The mission moved through Scotland, Ireland and England and ended in London from March 1875, and he left England on 14 August 1875. His Chicago church and home had burned in the 1871 fire.
